title: Variables, constants and types
idea: A variable is a name for a value. `let` lets you reassign it; `const` does not. The value has the type, never the name.

analogy.text: A label stuck on a box. The label is the variable, the box holds the value. `let` lets you move the label to another box; `const` glues it down.
analogy.breaks: `const` locks the label, not the box: an object's contents can still change.

points: `let` and `const` are visible only inside their `{ }` block; `var` ignores blocks.
`const` needs a value when declared; a `let` without one starts as `undefined`.
`typeof` reports the type of whatever the variable holds right now.
Every value has a type, such as number or string. Later pages cover them.

hero.caption: Scope is where a name is visible. Redeclare means declaring the same name again in the same scope.

code.title: let, const and var
code.caption: Run it. Then change `const limit` to `let limit` and see what the `try` line does.

pitfalls: Avoid `var` in new code: it ignores block scope and leaks out of `if` and `for`.
Keep one type per variable: a number that becomes a string breaks later math.
Declare every variable with a keyword; a bare `total = 1` throws in modules.

quiz.why: `var i` ignores the loop's block, so `i` is 2 afterwards. `let j` exists only inside its loop, so `typeof j` is "undefined".

takeaway: Default to `const`, use `let` when needed, and skip `var`.
